I think the disappearance of this can be traced back to education. I've discussed this issue at length with my dad, who graduated high school in 1980. He will sometimes reference classic texts with the assumption that I know what he's talking about - but I was never required to read any of the things he references. Things like 1984, Brave New World, Civil Disobedience, On Liberty, Areopagitica, The Age of Reason, Common Sense, The Federalist Papers and the Anti-Federalist Papers, or even reading the source material for the Consitution and the Declaration of Independence. All of those are things he was required to read in high school, but during my time in high school we were given a brief synopsis of each, then made to read The Awakening, Huck Finn, and various Shakespeare works - and I went to a school that is one of the best in Iowa for academics, and is frequently ranked nationally.

It sounds simple, but people don't read anymore. Or if they do, it's of the fantasy, instant gratification variety. I didn't even know of the existence of many of those books and essays until I got to college and started watching lectures and debates from Christopher Hitchens. The number of things he always referred to made me realize how little I knew about valuable works from the past. Being interviewed on Sean Hannity's show on Fox News, Hitchens called out Hannity by saying, "You strike me as the sort of person who has never read any of the arguments against your position ever." I think that's true of most of society now, although maybe that has always been the case.

Hearing friends, family, and strangers discuss recent issues like the confederate flag or gay marriage makes me realize that so many people are starting from the beginning of the reasoning process, or maybe they're just picking up where CNN left of at the last commercial break. They don't have the benefit of considering arguments before they come up, which is one of the advantages of reading things which make you think. The way people frame arguments seems almost designed to ensure that the same discussion will be had again in a matter of months or years. People don't respond to the person they're arguing against, they rail against the type of person they've been trained to believe is their opposition. Suggest clemency for illegal immigrants and people will assume you also want to spend more on welfare and other entitlements, but in the same discussion you can suggest abolishing the minimum wage and they will assume you want to cut welfare and entitlements.

This is actually done not for reasons of political correctness or causing offense, but because of potential legal ramifications of certain words under international law.

Because of the legal concept of "co-belligerents", countries are very careful to avoid using certain terms that would indicate an act of war. A state considers itself at war with any country that is assisting a state that is at war. The US provides assistance to Ukraine. By acknowledging an "invasion", Russia would be at war with the US.

E-Prime (short for English-Prime, sometimes denoted É or E′), a prescriptive version of the English language, excludes all forms of the verb to be. E-Prime does not allow the conjugations of to be—be, am, is, are, was, were, been, being—the archaic forms of to be (e.g. art, wast, wert), or the contractions of to be—'m, 's, 're (e.g. I'm, he's, she's, they're).

Some scholars advocate using E-Prime as a device to clarify thinking and strengthen writing.[1] For example, the sentence "the film was good" could not be expressed under the rules of E-Prime, and the speaker might instead say "I liked the film" or "the film made me laugh". The E-Prime versions communicate the speaker's experience rather than judgment, making it harder for the writer or reader to confuse opinion with fact.
